calls.reason: The Verge confirms CNET corrected 41 of 77 AI-written stories. CNET's own note confirms editors reviewed the drafts and the errors still got through. Calling that inattention is a fair description, not a separate factual claim.
The corrections show false information was published, but no source shows why editors missed it. Marcus himself frames the mechanism as probable, and CNET describes active editing.

There are isolated 2023 incidents (Men's Journal, Gizmodo) and NewsGuard counts more AI content-farm sites. But nothing compares this to an earlier baseline, and Gizmodo's editors were bypassed rather than over-trusting.

A January 2023 study shows ChatGPT making up facts, and a survey shows early workplace use. But 'too many' is a value judgment, and nothing shows the limit is inherent or that people relied on its facts.

Stanford's AI Index reports 78% of organisations using AI in 2024, and Pew finds ChatGPT use doubled. Google admits errors in its widely deployed AI Overviews. Together that points to AI that is widespread yet fallible.
